list_servers.title: List MySQL flexible servers in the subscription
list_servers.description: Every Azure Database for MySQL flexible server in the subscription, with its version, SKU, storage, state and `fullyQualifiedDomainName` -- the host a client connects to. `state` of `Stopped` explains a server that is not answering without anything being wrong with it.

output.description: Every MySQL flexible server in the subscription.

items.description: id, name, location, sku and properties (version, state, fullyQualifiedDomainName, storage, backup, highAvailability, network).

list_servers_in_group.title: List MySQL servers in a resource group
list_servers_in_group.description: The MySQL flexible servers in one resource group, with the same detail as list_servers. Cheaper when the group is already known.

resource_group.description: The resource group to look in.

items.description: id, name, location, sku and properties.

get_server.title: Get a MySQL flexible server
get_server.description:
One server in full: MySQL version, compute SKU, storage size and whether auto-grow is on, backup retention and geo-redundancy, high-availability mode, network configuration and administrator login.
`storage.autoGrow` is worth checking early -- a server without it stops accepting writes the moment the disk fills, and the error MySQL returns does not say so.

server_name.description: The server name, without the .mysql.database.azure.com suffix.

sku.description: name and tier -- Burstable, GeneralPurpose or MemoryOptimized.

properties.description: version, state, fullyQualifiedDomainName, administratorLogin, storage, backup, highAvailability, network and replicationRole.

create_or_update_server.title: Create a MySQL flexible server
create_or_update_server.description:
Create a managed MySQL server, or replace an existing one's configuration. The name becomes part of a public DNS name and must be globally unique -- check_name_availability tests it first.
`administrator_login_password` is only meaningful at creation and is never readable afterwards; store it somewhere before making the call. Provisioning takes several minutes: poll get_server until `state` is `Ready`.
Storage can be grown later but never shrunk, and the compute tier can be changed with update_server.
create_or_update_server.notes: The server name must be globally unique. The admin password is only returned to you here -- never afterwards.

resource_group.description: The resource group to create the server in.

server_name.description: The server name -- globally unique, lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.

administrator_login.description: The MySQL administrator username. Cannot be changed later.

administrator_login_password.description: The administrator password. Only settable here and at update_server; never readable.

sku_name.description: Compute size, e.g. Standard_B1ms or Standard_D2ds_v4.

sku_tier.description: Compute tier. Burstable is the cheap one and throttles under sustained load.

storage_size_gb.description: Storage in GB. Can be grown later, never shrunk.

storage_auto_grow.description: Grow storage automatically as it fills. Without it, a full disk stops writes.

backup_retention_days.description: Days of automatic backup to keep, 1 to 35.

geo_redundant_backup.description: Replicate backups to the paired region. Fixed at creation.

high_availability_mode.description: ZoneRedundant or SameZone standby. Roughly doubles the compute cost.

output.description: The server as created; provisioning continues asynchronously.

properties.description: state -- Creating at this point -- and fullyQualifiedDomainName once ready.

update_server.title: Scale or reconfigure a MySQL server
update_server.description:
Merge a change into an existing server: a different compute SKU, more storage, a new backup retention, a rotated administrator password, or high availability on or off.
A compute SKU change restarts the server, so it is a brief outage. Storage can only grow. Turning high availability on provisions a standby and roughly doubles the compute bill.
update_server.notes: A SKU change restarts the server. Storage cannot be reduced.

sku_name.description: New compute size. Changing it restarts the server.

storage_size_gb.description: New storage size in GB. Must be larger than the current one.

storage_auto_grow.description: Turn storage auto-grow on or off.

backup_retention_days.description: New backup retention in days, 1 to 35.

administrator_login_password.description: Rotate the administrator password. Breaks anything using the old one.

high_availability_mode.description: Turn high availability on or off.

properties.description: state -- Updating while the change lands.

delete_server.title: Delete a MySQL server
delete_server.description: Destroy a MySQL flexible server, every database on it, and its automatic backups. Irreversible -- unlike Azure SQL there is no restorable-dropped list to recover from afterwards. Take a backup out of the server first if the data matters, or restore to a new server before deleting this one.
delete_server.notes: Deletes the server's backups as well. There is no recovery afterwards.

start_server.title: Start a stopped MySQL server
start_server.description: Bring a stopped server back online and resume compute billing. Asynchronous -- poll get_server until `state` is `Ready`. A server stopped for 7 days is started automatically by Azure whether you ask or not.

stop_server.title: Stop a MySQL server
stop_server.description: Stop the server, which halts compute billing; storage and backups keep billing. Every open connection is dropped and nothing can connect until start_server. Azure restarts a stopped server automatically after 7 days, so this is a way to save money overnight, not to mothball a server.
stop_server.notes: Drops all connections. Azure auto-starts the server after 7 days.

restart_server.title: Restart a MySQL server
restart_server.description:
Restart the server, which is what applies a static (non-dynamic) parameter change from update_configuration. Every connection is dropped and the server is unavailable for a minute or two.
On a high-availability server, setting restart_with_failover restarts by failing over to the standby instead, which is faster and is also how you test that the standby actually works.
restart_server.notes: Drops all connections. The server is unavailable while it restarts.

restart_with_failover.description: Restart by failing over to the standby. Only valid on a high-availability server.

max_failover_seconds.description: How long to allow the failover to take before giving up.

list_databases.title: List the schemas on a MySQL server
list_databases.description: Every database (schema) on the server, with its character set and collation. The MySQL system schemas -- `mysql`, `information_schema`, `performance_schema`, `sys` -- appear here too and are not yours to touch.

create_database.title: Create an empty schema on a MySQL server
create_database.description: Create a database (schema) on the server. It comes up empty -- creating tables, users and grants inside it needs a MySQL client, which this connector is not. `utf8mb4` with `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci` is the sane default charset on MySQL 8; `utf8` is the three-byte legacy one and will mangle emoji.

server_name.description: The server to create the schema on.

charset.description: Character set. utf8mb4 is full UTF-8; utf8 is the truncated legacy one.

collation.description: Collation, which decides sorting and comparison.

delete_database.title: Drop a schema from a MySQL server
delete_database.description: Drop a database and every table in it. Irreversible short of restoring the whole server from a backup to a new server -- there is no per-schema restore.

database_name.description: The schema to drop, with all its tables.

list_firewall_rules.title: List a MySQL server's firewall rules
list_firewall_rules.description:
The IP ranges allowed to reach the server. The first thing to check when a client times out rather than being rejected for a bad password. A rule with both addresses 0.0.0.0 is the "allow other Azure services" special case; a rule of 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 opens the server to the internet.
A server deployed into a virtual network has no firewall rules at all -- access is decided by the network instead.

create_firewall_rule.title: Allow an IP range to reach a MySQL server
create_firewall_rule.description:
Open the server to a range of client addresses. Keep it as narrow as the client needs -- 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 exposes the server to the whole internet, with only the MySQL password in the way.
This grants network reach only; the client still has to authenticate. Reusing a rule name replaces that rule.
create_firewall_rule.notes: Widening the range widens the attack surface. It grants no database privileges.

rule_name.description: A name for the rule. Reusing one replaces it.

start_ip_address.description: First address in the allowed range.

end_ip_address.description: Last address in the range; the same as the start for a single address.

delete_firewall_rule.title: Remove a MySQL firewall rule
delete_firewall_rule.description: Close a previously allowed range. Clients in it lose access on their next connection; existing connections are not cut, which makes the effect look delayed. Check list_firewall_rules first to see what the rule was carrying.

list_configurations.title: List a MySQL server's parameters
list_configurations.description:
Every MySQL server parameter with its current value, default, allowed values, and two flags that decide how you change it: `isDynamicConfig` (true means the change applies without a restart) and `isReadOnly` (true means it cannot be changed at all on a managed server).
This is `SHOW VARIABLES` plus the metadata you need to change one safely.

filter.description: Filter the parameter list, e.g. by keyword.

output.description: Every server parameter and its metadata.

items.description: name and properties (value, defaultValue, allowedValues, dataType, source, isDynamicConfig, isReadOnly).

update_configuration.title: Change a MySQL server parameter
update_configuration.description:
Set one server parameter -- `max_connections`, `slow_query_log`, `long_query_time`, `sql_mode` and the rest of `my.cnf`.
Check the parameter's `isDynamicConfig` in list_configurations first: a dynamic parameter takes effect immediately, a static one needs restart_server, which drops every connection. Setting `source` back to `system-default` reverts to Azure's default. Values outside `allowedValues` are rejected.
update_configuration.notes: A non-dynamic parameter only takes effect after restart_server, which drops all connections.

value.description: The new value. Must be within the parameter's allowedValues.

source.description: user-override applies your value; system-default reverts to Azure's.

properties.description: value, source and isDynamicConfig -- check the last one to know whether a restart is needed.

list_backups.title: List a MySQL server's backups
list_backups.description: The automatic backups Azure holds for the server, each with its completion time and type. These are what a point-in-time restore draws on; the retention window is `backup.backupRetentionDays` from get_server, and anything older is gone.

items.description: id, name and properties (backupType, completedTime, source).

restore_server_to_point_in_time.title: Restore a MySQL server to a point in time
restore_server_to_point_in_time.description:
Create a NEW server from an existing one's backups, as it stood at a given instant. Nothing is overwritten -- the source keeps running -- so this is safe to reach for mid-incident, and it is the only recovery path MySQL flexible server offers.
`restore_point_in_time` must be inside the source's backup retention window. Restores take a while; poll get_server on the new name until `state` is `Ready`. The restored server has its own firewall rules and parameters copied from the source.
restore_server_to_point_in_time.notes: Creates a second server, which bills separately from the source.

resource_group.description: The resource group to create the restored server in.

target_server_name.description: A name for the restored server. Globally unique, and must not already exist.

location.description: The region for the restored server.

source_server_id.description: ARM id of the server to restore from, from get_server.

restore_point_in_time.description: The instant to restore to, ISO 8601 UTC, inside the retention window.

properties.description: state -- Creating while the restore runs.

list_replicas.title: List a MySQL server's read replicas
list_replicas.description: The read replicas of a server, each with its own SKU, region and state. Replicas serve read traffic and lag behind the source; the `replicationRole` on each says whether it is a Source or a Replica. Deleting the source promotes nothing automatically -- plan a failover before you need one.

items.description: id, name, location, sku and properties (replicationRole, sourceServerResourceId, state).

check_name_availability.title: Check whether a MySQL server name is free
check_name_availability.description: MySQL flexible server names become public DNS names, so they share one global namespace. This asks whether a name is available before a create fails on it, and the `reason` distinguishes an invalid name from a taken one.

output.description: Whether the name is available, and why not if it is not.

nameAvailable.description: True when the name can be used.
